newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spain's 18-mo bill seen pleasing investment trusts.
newsitem.headline: Spain's 18-mo bill seen pleasing investment trusts.

text.p: The Treasury said Spain's new 18-month bills, set to debut on April 28, are aimed at the fast-growing industry of investment trusts, and dealers expect the funds to snap up the new instrument.

"The significant reduction in public debt yields during 1996, and the Spanish yield curve suggest it would be advisable to increase the range of instruments in which (short-term fixed-rate funds) can invest," officials at the Treasury Ministry said on Wednesday.
FIAMM, funds which invest in fixed-rate public annd private paper with maturities of up to 18 months, should be attracted to the higher-yielding paper.
"In this way FIAMM could buy public paper at higher yields than one-year and six-month bills," the Treasury added.
"It seems the Treasury is aiming to please investment trusts," a money market dealer said.

The 18-month Treasury bills will be the longest assets that this kind of investment fund can buy without paying withholding tax, market sources added. While investors have to pay a 25 percent witholding tax on public notes and bonds, Spanish bills are not subjected to such a tax.
At the end of March, investment trusts' total assets were around 21.33 trillion pesetas, up 500 billion from the previous month thanks to new savings and to higher market prices.
FIAMM assets alone at the end of the first quarter stood at around 8.54 trillion pesetas, plus an additional 1.19 trillion in FIAMMs devoted solely to public assets.
By adding another short-term instrument to its repetoire, the Spanish Treasury hopes to face competition from other sovereign issuers better.
"There are financial instruments with short maturity issued by sovereign issuers with which the Spanish Treasury has to compete to get money," the Treasury officials said.
On the Italian market, normally considered an alternative to the Spanish market by foreign investors, 18-month deep discount bills, called CTZ, have been offered since January 1997.
The issuance of the new instrument also stems from the Treasury's wish to maintain the current average life of Spanish public debt.
After the issuance of six-month bills was resumed in September 1996, Spain's average debt life fell slightly by end 1996 to 3.76 years from 3.89 twelve months before.
"The issuance of 18-months bills will allow us to compensate for this fall in average life, through a diversified offer of maturity in the short end," the Treasury said.
The first auction of 18-month bills is scheduled on Monday April 28. After that, they will be offered twice a month on the same days as the one-year bill auctions.
